[[File:Hakea salicifolia.jpg|thumb|New growth]]

'''''Hakea salicifolia''''', commonly known as the '''willow-leaved hakea''',<ref name="RBGS">{{cite web |title=''Hakea salicifolia'' |url=https://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Hakea~salicifolia |publisher=Royal Botanic Garden Sydney |access-date=28 September 2020}}</ref> is a species of flowering plant that is [[Endemism|endemic]] to eastern Australia. It is an adaptable, fast growing small tree or shrub with attractive foliage and cream white flowers.

==Description==
''Hakea salicifolia'' is a fast-growing upright shrub or small tree to {{convert|3-5|m|ft|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} tall. Smaller branches are smooth with obvious dark red longitudinal ribbing. Young shoots have sparse silky hairs or may be totally hairless. Leaves are narrowly oval shaped, widest in the middle up to 12 cm long and {{convert|5-20|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} wide tapering to a point or occasionally rounded at the apex. The pale green leaves are smooth, occasionally bluish-green with a powdery film. Young leaves are darker with sparse flattened silky white and rusty coloured hairs quickly becoming smooth. The [[inflorescence]] consists of a single [[umbel]] of 16–28 white to pale yellow flowers on a short stalk {{convert|1-1.5|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long. The young flower [[bract]]s are {{convert|3|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long and slightly hairy externally. The [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicel]] is {{convert|4.5-7|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long. The [[perianth]] is smooth, bluish-green with a powdery film and {{convert|2.3-3.5|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long. The [[style (botany)|style]] {{convert|6-6.5|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long. Egg-shaped fruit are {{convert|2.3-3.5|cm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|1.3-3|cm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} wide narrowing gradually to a slightly upturned beak with small horns. The fruit surface is covered with black blister-like warts {{convert|1-5|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} high.<ref name="DUI">{{cite book |last1=Holliday |first1=Ivan |title="Hakeas a Field and Garden Guide" |publisher=Reed New Holland |isbn=1-877069-14-0}}</ref><ref name="W & F">{{cite book |last1=Wriggley |first1=John W. |last2=Fagg |first2=Murray |title="Australian Native Plants-Propagation, cultivation and use in landscaping" |date=1996 |publisher=Reed New Holland |isbn=1-876334-30-4}}</ref><ref name="FOAB">{{cite book |editor-last=Wilson |editor-first=Annette |last1=Barker |first1=Robyn M. |last2=Haegi |first2=Laurence A. |last3=Barker |first3=William R. |title="Flora of Australia" Vol.17B Proteaceae 3 Hakea to Dryandra |date=1999 |publisher=ABRS |isbn=0-643-06454-0}}</ref>
[[File:Willow-leaved Hakea seed.jpg|thumb|225px|Fruit]]

==Taxonomy and naming==
Willow-leaved hakea was first formally described in 1800 by French botanist [[Étienne Pierre Ventenat]] who gave it the name ''Embrothium salicifolium'' and published the description in {{Lang|fr|Description des Plantes Nouvelles et peu connues, cultivees dans le Jardin de J.M. Cels}}. The [[Type (biology)|type]] specimen was grown in the garden of [[Jacques Philippe Martin Cels]] from material collected from [[Botany Bay]] in 1792.<ref name=APNI1>{{cite web|title=''Embothrium salicifolium''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/543975|publisher=APNI|access-date=5 February 2019}}</ref><ref name="Vent.">{{cite book |last1=Ventenat |first1=Etienne Pierre |title=Description des plantes nouvelles et peu connues : cultivées dans le jardin de J.M. Cels : avec figures |date=1800 |location=Paris |page=t8 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/133288#page/49/mode/1up |access-date=5 February 2019}}</ref>  In 1941, English botanist [[Brian Burtt]] changed the name to ''Hakea salicifolia'' and published the description in ''Bulletin of Miscellaneous Information''.<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Hakea salicifolia''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/526054|publisher=APNI|access-date=5 February 2019}}</ref> The [[specific epithet]] ''(salicifolia)'' is derived from the [[Latin]] words {{Lang|la|salix}}<ref name="RWB">{{cite book|author-link1=Roland W. Brown|last1=Brown|first1=Roland Wilbur|title=The Composition of Scientific Words|date=1956|publisher=Smithsonian Institution Press|location=Washington, D.C.}}</ref>{{rp|174}} meaning "willow" and {{Lang|la|folium}} meaning "leaf"<ref name="RWB" />{{rp|46}} referring to the willow-like leaves.<ref name="SAF">{{cite web |title=''Hakea salicifolia'' |url=http://www.flora.sa.gov.au/efsa/lucid/Hakea/key/Australian%20Hakea%20species/Media/Html/Hakea_salicifolia_ssp._salicifolia.htm |website=Flora of South Australian:Online |publisher=South Australian Government |access-date=5 February 2019}}</ref>

Two subspecies are currently recognised by the [[Australian Plant Census]]:
*''Hakea salicifolia'' <small>(Vent.) B.L.Burtt</small> subsp. ''salicifolia'' that has leaves more than {{cvt|7|mm}} wide and grows on the coast and ranges from [[Springbrook, Queensland]] to [[Jervis Bay, New South Wales]];<ref name="APC1">{{cite web |title=''Hakea salicifolia'' subsp. ''salicifolia'' |url=https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/apc-format/display/164891 |website=Australian Plant Census |access-date=28 September 2020}}</ref>
*''Hakea salicifolia'' subsp. ''angustifolia'' <small>([[A.A.Ham.]]) [[W.R.Barker]]</small> that has leaves {{cvt|4–7|mm}} wide and grows near water courses between [[Hornsby, New South Wales|Hornsby]] and [[Helensburgh, New South Wales|Helensburgh]] in the Sydney region.<ref name="APC2">{{cite web |title=''Hakea salicifolia'' subsp. ''angustifolia'' |url=https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/apc-format/display/164892 |website=Australian Plant Census |access-date=28 September 2020}}</ref><ref name="FOAB"/>

''Hakea saligna'' var. ''angustifolia'' was first formally described in 1920 by [[Arthur Andrew Hamilton]] in ''[[Linnean Society of New South Wales|Proceedings of the Linnean Society of New South Wales]]''<ref name=APNI3>{{cite web|title=''Hakea saligna'' var. ''angustifolia''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/526132|publisher=APNI|access-date=28 September 2020}}</ref><ref name="A.A.Ham.">{{cite journal |last1=Hamilton |first1=Arthur Andrew |title=Notes from the Botanic Gardens, Sydney. |journal=Proceedings of the Linnean Society of New South Wales |date=1920 |volume=45 |issue=2 |pages=261–262 |doi=10.5962/bhl.part.19545 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/24141#page/303/mode/1up |access-date=28 September 2020}}</ref> before being renamed ''Hakea salicifolia'' subsp. ''angustifolia'' in 1999 by [[William Robert Barker]].<ref name=APNI4>{{cite web|title=''Hakea salicifolia'' var. ''angustifolia''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/558787|publisher=APNI|access-date=28 September 2020}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Hakea salicifolia'' is a widespread species growing mainly from [[Kempsey, New South Wales|Kempsey]] to the [[Shoalhaven River]], [[Dorrigo, New South Wales|Dorrigo]], [[Whian Whian, New South Wales|Whian Whian]] and the [[Blue Mountains (New South Wales)|Blue Mountains]]. Also found near the [[Queensland]] and [[New South Wales]] border. Grows in wet sclerophyll forest often near rainforest.<ref name="FOAB"/><ref name="PNET">{{cite web |title=''Hakea salicifolia'' |url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Hakea~salicifolia |website=PlantNET:NSW Flora Online |access-date=5 February 2019 |ref=Royal Botanic Gardens & Domain Trust}}</ref> 

==Ecology==
Willow-leaved Hakea is an [[invasive plant species]] in [[New Zealand]] and is listed by the [[New Zealand Department of Conservation]] as one of about 300 environmental weeds. It is also invasive in [[Portugal]].<ref name="almeida">{{Cite journal |url=http://revistas.ucm.es/index.php/BOCM/article/view/BOCM0606110117A/6271 |title=Exotic naturalized flora of continental Portugal – A reassessment |last1=Domingues de Almeida |first1=João |last2=Freitas |first2=Helena |journal=Botanica Complutensis |year=2006 |series=30 |volume=30 |pages=117–130 |issn=0214-4565 |access-date=13 April 2017}}</ref>{{rp|123}} An attractive ornamental tree adaptable to most soils and aspects from sub-tropical to temperate zones creating issues with over abundance of the species in some localities. Planted on tea plantations in [[Tanzania]] as a wind-break and boundary hedge.<ref name="W & F"/><ref>{{cite book|last=Howell|first=Clayson|title=Consolidated list of environmental weeds in New Zealand|publisher=Department of Conservation|location=Wellington|date=May 2008|series=DRDS292|url=http://www.doc.govt.nz/upload/documents/science-and-technical/drds292.pdf|isbn=978-0-478-14413-0|access-date=15 January 2013}}</ref><ref name="POWO">{{cite web |title=''Hakea salicifolia'' |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:704322-1 |website=Plants of the World Online |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew |access-date=6 February 2019}}</ref>
